FREELANCE EDITOR QUOTE CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Quote an editing job: flat fee, per-word rate, and what happens if the manuscript is slower than you thought

Enter the word count, the level of edit and the hourly rate you need. You get the flat fee, the per-word and per-page equivalents clients compare, the working days the job needs, a rush surcharge, and what your fee pays per hour if you edit slower than planned.

Paces are in words per hour and you can change them. It works backwards from the income you want; it does not know market rates.

The job

Fill in the job, then click Work out the quote.

What it does, and what it leaves to you

    
    
      
  • Counts: edit hours = words / (words per hour / condition factor of 0.85 clean, 1 average, 1.3 rough); billable hours = (edit hours + extra hours) plus the admin percentage; fee = billable hours times your rate, plus the rush surcharge when the deadline is inside your rush window.
    • 
      
  • Not decided: what the market pays, your real words per hour (time yourself on a sample), sales tax or VAT, contract terms, payment schedule, kill fees, and whether the client's text needs the level they asked for.
    • 
    

  


  

    
Common questions

    
How do I price an editing job?

    
Estimate the hours, then multiply by the hourly rate you need. Hours are the word count divided by how many words per hour you edit at that level, adjusted for how rough the text is, plus admin time and any extras such as a style sheet. Quote the result as a flat fee and state the per-word equivalent, because clients compare per-word.

    
What are typical editing speeds?

    
They vary a lot with the person and the text. The defaults here are rule-of-thumb figures: about 2,000 words an hour for proofreading, 1,000 for copyediting, 600 for line editing and 350 for developmental editing. They are inputs, so replace them with your own timed pace.

    
Why charge a flat fee instead of hourly?

    
Clients usually want a number up front. A flat fee is safe only if your pace estimate is right, so the page shows what the fee pays per hour if you work slower than planned and suggests a cap on scope or an overage clause.

    
When should I add a rush fee?

    
When the deadline is shorter than your normal turnaround and displaces other work. Enter the working days the client gives and the window below which you charge extra; the surcharge percentage is yours to set.

    
Does it know market rates?

    
No. It works backwards from the hourly income you want. Compare the per-word result with published rate surveys from editors' associations before you send a quote.

    
Is my manuscript or my rate uploaded anywhere?

    
No. Only a word count and your own numbers are entered, everything is worked out in your browser and nothing is sent; a test in the code asserts there are no network calls.

Your figures. This page runs in your browser and sends nothing anywhere; closing the tab discards them, and downloads are files on your own device.

    
Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record: nothing you enter is saved anywhere.

    
Everything runs in your browser. Your figures are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (analysis_run, example_loaded, summary_downloaded, csv_downloaded) are counted only in local storage on your device, never with any of your data, and are switched off by Do Not Track.
